posts.title: Judging the evidence, or whose side people are on
posts.body:
Court filings unsealed last month show Meta employees discussing a whisper strategy against Jonathan Haidt.

Nobody has shown it was ever carried out.

The notes come from a meeting in March 2023. They talk about turning academics against him and finding someone to write a piece attacking his work. They're also full of typos and shorthand, and they read more like a brainstorm than a plan. Meta hasn't commented.

Ugly and unproven, both at once.

Then the story turned.

Candice Odgers is one of the researchers who has challenged Haidt's conclusions. She says The Times suggested that she and other critics were paid by Meta to do it.

Her answer was flat. Meta doesn't fund her research. She's never been approached by Meta to shape what she says publicly.

Her name isn't in those Meta documents. The link was made by the reader, not the filing.

And that's where I have a problem, because the reasoning runs backwards. Her findings are inconvenient, therefore her motives must be bought.

She's Chancellor's Professor of Psychology and Informatics at UC Irvine. Twenty five years on child and adolescent mental health, her own count. Her review of The Anxious Generation ran in Nature.

That doesn't make her right.

It makes her someone you answer rather than someone you discredit.

And she isn't out on a limb. The National Academies, December 2023: available research linking social media to health "shows small effects and weak associations". The same report says its review "did not support the conclusion that social media causes changes in adolescent health at the population level".

That committee also said the evidence isn't robust enough to settle it. Which cuts at my own confidence, and I'll take it.

I've had a small taste of what happens when you question the size of an effect. Someone decides you're defending Big Tech.

I'm not.

I want harmful design challenged, and I want researchers free to challenge a popular claim. Both.

Meta's motives deserve scrutiny. So does Haidt's evidence. So does Odgers' evidence. Nobody gets a free pass.

Next I'm going through Haidt's recent interviews and the headlines built on them, to separate what the research shows from what it doesn't. Not to wave away real harm, and not to carry water for the platforms.

With the UK moving towards under sixteen restrictions, parents need perspective as much as children need protection.

If an argument should be judged on its evidence rather than on who is making it, repost this.

Are we still judging the evidence, or have we started judging whose side people are on?

posts.title: A face scan to get into an app
posts.body:
A ban on social media under 16 needs a way to know who is 16, and Ofcom's shortlist is a passport, digital ID, bank check or face scan.

I'm not sure parents have been asked what they think of that.

Take each in turn. A passport or driving licence works for most people, though the estimate doing the rounds is that 150,000 sixteen and seventeen year olds hold neither, and that one comes from CitizenCard out of a survey Ofcom itself calls non representative. A bank check covers about 90 percent of that age group, which leaves around one in ten outside it. A face scan has a margin of error at 16, which is why Ofcom wants a challenge age and a second check. And a digital ID means doing the photo ID step once, then reusing it.

Each one fixes a problem and hands over something else.

A child's face, a child's bank details, or a new ID that sits behind every app.

The people who want the ban have a fair answer. Checks are the price of a rule that means something, and the alternative is the system we have now, which is a box a child ticks.

I can hold both of those at once. What I can't tell you is where the line is for your child, and neither can Ofcom. Its four methods are the ones it says are currently capable of working, and it'll consult on draft guidance once the regulations are laid in Parliament.

So the live question isn't only whether there should be a ban. It's what you'd be willing to hand over to make it work.

This is the ban series continued.

Repost it if you would rather the numbers here were traced than repeated.

Would you let your child use a face scan or a bank check to get into an app, and what would you want promised in return?

posts.title: Four ways to prove you are 16
posts.body:
Ofcom has named four ways to check that a UK user is 16, and says no method is "completely robust against circumvention by children".

It published the assessment on 29 October, while Parliament works out how the under sixteen ban will run in practice.

The four are photo ID matching, digital ID services, banking based checks and facial age estimation. Ofcom's phrase for them is methods currently capable of being highly effective, and "currently" is doing work in that sentence.

Then the numbers that decide who actually gets through. An estimated 94 percent of people aged 16 and over hold a passport or driving licence. About 90 percent of sixteen and seventeen year olds hold a bank account. For those who hold neither document, the figure doing the rounds is 150,000, which comes from CitizenCard rather than Ofcom, out of a school survey Ofcom itself calls non representative. Treat it as an order of magnitude.

On face scanning, Ofcom doesn't publish an error in years. What it says is that services should use a challenge age, checking anyone who scans close to the line a second way.

To be fair, none of this says the ban can't work. A ban with real checks is a better ban than one without them, and this is a serious piece of work.

But look at what a check does. It decides who gets through the door.

Nothing more.

It doesn't decide what a fifteen year old does with a friend's login, or what they feel when something odd lands in their feed.

Ofcom says it'll publish research on circumvention within twelve months of the ban coming into effect. Until then, what a child understands about why the rule exists is doing a lot of the work.

That's the part I build, so I'm not neutral. I'd still say the same thing without it: a deadline is not a plan.

This is the ban series continued.

Repost this if you want the checks argued over before they land rather than after.

If your child is twelve now, what do you want them to understand by the day the checks start?

posts.title: Twenty five thousand teenagers and the lag
posts.body:
A study of 25,629 teenagers in Greater Manchester found no evidence that time on social media predicted later emotional difficulties.

It followed the same young people for three years, surveying them each autumn from 2021 to 2023. The team is at the University of Manchester, and it was published in the Journal of Public Health in March 2026.

The method matters. It separates what happens to a child from how children differ from each other, then asks one narrow thing: whether more social media this year predicts more emotional difficulty next year. For girls and for boys, the answer was no. The same went for gaming.

Now the honest part. This isn't a finding of no link at all. At the same moment in time, more social media went with slightly more emotional difficulty, and the paper calls it small. What it didn't find is that the one comes before the other.

And the limits are the authors' own. Everything was self reported. It measured hours, not what the hours were spent on. The gap between surveys was a year, which can hide shorter term effects. The average age at the start was about twelve and a half, so this says nothing about a nine year old.

The press release went further than the paper. It said social media and gaming did not cause symptoms. The paper says they may not play a causal role.

That's a smaller claim, and the right one.

Add it to the others. Different teams, different countries, a small effect each time.

This is The Wrong Villain series continued.

What it leaves open is the part parents actually live with. Not how long, but what, and who with, and what happened after.

Twenty five thousand teenagers is a lot of evidence to ignore because it found nothing. Worth a repost.

If hours is the wrong measure, what would you want researchers to count instead?
posts.comment: The paper: Cheng, Panayiotou, Finseras, Andersen and Humphrey, "How do social media use, gaming frequency, and internalizing symptoms predict each other over time in early-to-middle adolescence?", Journal of Public Health, volume 48, issue 1, March 2026, online December 2025. Sample 25,629 from the #BeeWell cohort in Greater Manchester, three annual waves, autumn 2021 to 2023. Outcome is the emotional difficulties scale of Me and My Feelings, which is a symptom score and not a diagnosis of anxiety or depression. The lagged paths from social media to later symptoms were not significant for girls or boys (for girls, b of minus 0.001 with a 95 percent interval of minus 0.009 to 0.006). Same wave associations were small but present. Two things I could not check: the supplementary tables on active versus passive use, and anything about heavy users as a group, because the paper treats hours as a continuous measure. University of Manchester release, 14 January 2026. The sourced breakdown behind this series: guidedchildhood.com/v/li-1029-beewell

posts.title: The chatbot confidant
posts.body:
Twelve percent of American teenagers have already asked a chatbot for emotional support or advice.

Fifty four percent have used one for help with schoolwork.

Both numbers are from the Pew Research Center, 1,458 teenagers aged 13 to 17, surveyed in autumn 2025. These are American teenagers, not British ones, and "used it once" isn't "relies on it".

There are two readings of that twelve percent and I hold both on different days.

One says a teenager typing a worry into a machine at midnight is a child who didn't have, or didn't trust, a person to tell. The machine is the symptom, and it's a machine built to keep the conversation going.

The other says that for some young people, saying it first to something with no face is a way of practising. Rehearsing the sentence before they say it to a parent. That isn't nothing.

I don't think the survey can tell us which one it is. Nobody has followed these children for long enough to find out.

What I do think is that the difference comes down to what happens next. Whether the conversation ends with a person, or ends with another conversation.

So the one question I ask about any tool a child talks to isn't whether it's safe.

Safety is the floor.

It's whether it points back to a human when it matters.

Repost it if the real question is where the conversation ends, not whether the tool is safe.

Parents, which is it in your house: a place to practise, or a place to hide?

US only. I have not seen an equivalent UK figure I would trust and I would welcome one. I wrote the two readings in the post as equals on purpose; if the practising reading is wrong I would like to hear why.

posts.title: Half of UK children have an AI toy
posts.body:
Parents in the UK say half of their children have already been given an AI toy or learning device.

Thirty eight percent own two or more.

That comes from a May 2026 survey of 1,000 UK parents by FocalData, published by the British Standards Institution. It's a parent survey, so it's what parents report, not what children say. And "AI enabled toy or learning device" covers a lot, from a spelling tutor to a bear that talks back.

So it doesn't mean half of children are in danger. It means a category most of us haven't thought hard about is already in the house.

The talking one is what I keep coming back to. Common Sense Media, which surveyed American parents earlier this year, found nearly half had bought or considered buying one. Their advice is that no child aged five or under should use an AI toy at all, and that parents should take care with ages six to twelve.

A toy that answers every question, never gets tired and never says "not now" is teaching a child something about what a relationship is.

A seven year old can't see that for themselves.

Nobody has told most parents what to look for, and the survey says as much: the BSI headline is about gaps in guidance.

Four things a child should be able to tell you. Who's on the other side of this. What it remembers. What it can't do. When to go and find a person. We teach a short lesson on exactly that for younger children, and it starts from the idea that the child should be able to explain it to you.

An age on a box won't do that for us.

More parents should know what that survey actually said. Repost it.

If a toy in your house could talk back tomorrow, what's the first thing you'd want to know about it?

posts.title: The age is the easy part
posts.body:
I have built a product around the word readiness and I still cannot tell you how to test it.

That is the uncomfortable centre of this, and picking a better age does not make it go away.

Everyone argues about the number. Thirteen for an account. Sixteen for social media. Eighteen for an AI companion. I understand why. An age is enforceable, auditable, the same for every child, and a regulator can write it down.

What an age cannot do is describe the child in front of you. I know this, having three very different children.

One child can turn thirteen without knowing that an AI which sounds caring does not care. Without understanding that a chatbot can be confidently wrong about something it has no business being confident about. Without noticing when a conversation is being kept going rather than finished. With no idea when to stop talking to a machine and go and find a person.

So what would a readiness test actually look like.

Not a quiz. A child can pass a quiz on Monday and hand over their address on Friday. Not a certificate either, because the whole point is that it moves as they grow and as the technology does.

The closest I have got is three things a parent can see for themselves. Can the child explain, in their own words, why this thing is showing them this. Can they tell you about a time they stopped. And do they come to you when something turns, which depends entirely on whether coming to you went well enough last time that they would do it again.

That last one is the real test, and it is not about the child at all.

Our stage check is an attempt at this and I will not dress it up as more. Three questions about your own child, and a stage with the things worth practising next. A starting point rather than a measurement. We have no outcome evidence that a child who finishes a stage behaves differently afterwards, and almost nobody in this field does.

An age tells you when the door opens. It tells you nothing about who walks through it.

If you have ever asked for an age and wanted a plan, repost this.

If you had to judge whether a child was ready for something online, what would you actually look at?
posts.comment: Where the three ages come from, since the card leans on them. Thirteen is the platform minimum in most terms of service, which traces back to the United States children's privacy law rather than to any finding about thirteen year olds. Sixteen is the UK social media restriction, announced June 2026 with enforcement from 2027. Eighteen is Character.AI, which ended open ended chats for under eighteens from 25 November 2025 after lawsuits and an FTC inquiry, replacing them with a narrower creative experience. Three different answers about the same child, each arrived at by a different route, and none of them derived from evidence about what a child at that age can actually do. On our own stage check, I meant the line in the post literally: we have no outcome evidence that a child who finishes a stage behaves differently afterwards. It is three questions and a starting point, not a measurement, and I would rather say that than imply otherwise. If anyone knows of a readiness instrument for children online that has been tested against what children actually do later, I would genuinely like to read it.

posts.title: Fear is the engine on both sides now
posts.body:
A study everyone is quoting this week says 85 percent of Australian teenagers got round the under sixteen ban.

It doesn't say that.

The paper is in the BMJ, from the University of Newcastle. It recruited 436 adolescents and followed up with 408 of them three months after the ban began. What it found is that more than 85 percent of under sixteens were still using the platforms, mostly on accounts they already had.

Still using is not the same as broke in.

And the regulator's own follow up, 803 children, found the thing nobody is quoting. The share who actually held an account fell from 52.4 percent to 42.1 percent. eSafety calls that modest and statistically significant. It's the one measurable thing the ban has done so far, and it's missing from both arguments.

None of this means the ban works. The same paper says there isn't enough evidence of a real drop in use, its own authors say the full picture may take a decade, and it's one Australian state with self reported answers.

Jonathan Haidt made the loudest case of the decade out of alarm. A generation rewired. An epidemic with a start date. A conclusion that keeps arriving ahead of the effect sizes that would carry it.

The people who spend their days correcting him have started doing the same thing. A Psychology Today piece this month cited that BMJ paper as proof the ban failed.

The paper doesn't say the ban failed. It says we can't tell yet.

So fear is the engine on both sides now. One side is frightened of the phones. The other is frightened of the ban. Both reach past what the study will carry, because a careful answer doesn't move anybody.

Britain has this argument next and the law lands in 2027.

Which leaves a parent somewhere else entirely. The ban will do whatever it does. What happens in your house between now and the day it lands is the part nobody is legislating.

This is The Wrong Villain series continued.

Repost it if you are tired of being frightened by both sides.

What would actually change your mind about the ban?
posts.comment: Sources, and where I have been careful. The study is Barnes et al., BMJ 2026;393:e363695, University of Newcastle, published 24 June 2026. It recruited 436 adolescents aged 12 to under 17 and followed up with 408 of them three months in. It reports that more than 85 percent of under sixteens were still using platforms covered by the Act, mostly through accounts they already held, and finds insufficient evidence of a substantive early reduction. Its own authors say the full impacts may not be evident for a decade. It is one Australian state, the answers are self reported, and the confidence intervals are wide enough that modest effects cannot be ruled out, which is exactly why it cannot carry the weight either camp puts on it. The regulator's figures are the eSafety Commissioner's three month follow up, published July 2026, which surveyed 803 children aged 10 to 15: 85.9 percent using at least one age restricted platform before the ban and 81.5 percent after, measured with or without an account, and account ownership down from 52.4 percent to 42.1 percent, which eSafety calls modest but statistically significant. eSafety also says plainly that the report is not an assessment of whether platforms complied. The Psychology Today piece is Emma Bruehlman-Senecal, Why Banning Social Media Won't Fix Teen Mental Health, 15 October 2026, and it is worth reading: it is right that age checks create their own privacy problem, and right that for some children these platforms are where they find people like them. My disagreement is with one line, where the BMJ paper is cited as teenagers circumventing the ban. Continued use on an existing account is not circumvention, and the paper does not test whether the ban failed. On Jonathan Haidt, the thing he is right about is that parents are not imagining the problem. Where I part company is the size of the effect and the confidence of the conclusion. UK timing: the government has said enforcement from 2027, and a firmer date has been reported but I have not verified it, so I have said 2027.

posts.title: A ban is already teaching. The question is what.
posts.body:
Nobody can tell you yet whether banning under sixteens from social media works. Australia can already tell you what it teaches.

Its regulator went back three months after the ban began and surveyed 803 children. Before it, nearly 86 percent were using at least one age restricted platform. After, still above 81 percent. A separate study in the BMJ, 436 adolescents, found insufficient evidence that use had meaningfully fallen.

Then look at how. The BMJ study found fake accounts, someone else's account, private browsing. The regulator found something blunter. Half the children who still had accounts said the platform had never checked their age, and 37 percent had simply put themselves down as sixteen or over.

That's a child's first real lesson in digital life, and a law delivered it.

Identity online is something you assert, and nobody checks.

We've been teaching it longer than the law has, mind. A 2011 survey of a thousand American parents found a third whose child had joined Facebook before turning thirteen, and two thirds of those parents helped set the account up. I'm in no position to be smug: we used YouTube as a babysitter to get through the Covid days with two small girls at home. Parents were always the teacher here. A ban only changes the syllabus.

None of which makes the ban wrong. A protected period is worth having. A deadline is not a plan, but it isn't nothing either.

What it buys is time. What nobody is answering is what the time is for.

France's constitutional council struck down the under fifteen ban at the heart of its own new law in August. A blanket ban on every under fifteen, whatever the child and whatever the service, was out of proportion. And parliament had written no safeguards for a scheme that, to work at all, makes every user prove their age, adults included.

Britain has its own version coming in 2027, and the argument will be the same one.

Both sides are counting the same thing. Whether children got in. Whether children were kept out.

Nobody is counting what a sixteen year old can actually do.

Years ago my son was watching a dance video and wouldn't come off it, and I threatened to take away Saturday football. I knew inside a minute I'd got it wrong, and what stayed with me wasn't the row. It was that I had nothing to give him instead.

A ban switches the device off. It doesn't sit down with your child.

A ban teaches children something whatever we intend. Repost this if you would rather we chose what.

So if the door opens on your child's sixteenth birthday, what do you want them to come and tell you first?

Account ownership did fall, 52.4 percent to 42.1 percent, which eSafety calls modest but statistically significant, and eSafety says plainly that the report is not an assessment of whether platforms complied. The reasons children gave come from that same report: about half said the platform never checked their age, 37 percent had listed their age as 16 or above, 18 percent said they were wrongly estimated as over 16. The circumvention routes are a different source, the University of Newcastle study in the BMJ, which recruited 436 adolescents aged 12 to under 17 and followed up with 408 three months later. Its reported categories are fake accounts at 15 to 19 percent, someone else's account at 9 to 29 percent, private browsing at 6 to 11 percent and VPN use at only 2 to 3 percent, which is worth saying because VPNs are what everyone assumes. The paper found insufficient evidence of a substantive early reduction, and its own authors say the full impacts may not be clear for a decade. posts.title: Five years ago I would have shared that post
posts.body:
Five years ago I would have shared the Sweden story without checking it. Screens out of classrooms, printed textbooks back in.

I thought screens were mostly bad for children and that school should stay close to paper and pen, so a country as digital as Sweden turning round would have gone straight onto my feed. I changed my mind since, and not into the opposite camp, which is the part that takes longer.

The policy is real. In 2023 Sweden threw out its own national digitisation plan. In 2024 it funded printed textbooks. From July 2025, under twos in preschool use analogue materials only. All of that is accurate.

Here is what the viral version leaves out.

Sweden's own education agency never called it a crisis.

Three Swedish researchers went back through how the 2021 reading results were presented. The National Agency for Education emphasised the positives. The government called it a reading crisis. Sweden had in fact moved up the league table and declined less than most countries did.

And the two of them named different culprits. The agency said the main problem in Swedish schooling was segregation. The government said digitalisation, migration, and not enough time spent reading.

Only one of those is a villain you can fix with a book order.

Nobody has shown the books worked either. There is no evaluation, and PISA in September had Swedish reading down 21 points. I am not using that against the policy, because those students were born in 2009 and were schooled before the reform. It judges nothing.

The research is thinner than the story too. Paper does beat screen for reading, by about a fifth of a standard deviation across 54 studies. Look only at children and it halves, with a confidence interval that still includes zero. The handwriting brain study everyone quotes tested 36 university students.

So a government threw out one plan for not being evidence based, and replaced it with another that is not evidence based. Same move, opposite direction, and far better press.

The fight in my house was never about which book my son was reading. It was about the thing in his hand that kept asking for him back. No book order reaches that.

A school can change its tools. A parent cannot. So my bet, and I will call it a bet, is on teaching a child to notice it.

Repost it if you have ever shared something and checked it afterwards.

What actually changed in your house, the device or the rules around it?

The crisis framing: Reimers, Martin Bylund and Stenliden, Constructions of a reading crisis, Discourse: Studies in the Cultural Politics of Education, 2025, which documents that the National Agency for Education emphasised the positives of PIRLS 2021 while the government called it a crisis, that Sweden moved up the league table and declined less than most countries, and that the agency named segregation where the government named digitalisation and migration. Policy: the digitisation plan was scrapped in May 2023 for not being sufficiently evidence based, and an ordinance in force from 1 July 2025 restricts non analogue tools in preschool. Textbook funding is reported at around 2.1 billion kronor, though figures vary between reports, so I have said reported rather than confirmed. PISA 2025 published 8 September 2026: Sweden reading 466, down 21, against an OECD average that fell 14 to 463, and those students were born in 2009. Reading: Delgado and colleagues 2018, g = 0.21 across 54 studies and 171,055 students, and Furenes, Kucirkova and Bus 2021 for the child specific figure near 0.10 with a confidence interval including zero. Handwriting: Van der Weel and Van der Meer 2024, 36 university students, and a 2025 commentary by Pinet and Longcamp disputes the learning claim. On classroom devices generally, Ferguson's 2025 paper is titled Smartphone bans in schools remain unproven, and the English study of 1,227 students across 30 schools found no difference in attainment or wellbeing, so I am not arguing for a ban either. What I am not claiming: that Sweden acted in bad faith, that publishers drove this, or that the reading decline is invented. Reading difficulties among Swedish 10 year olds are reported to have risen from 12 to 19 percent in five years and the pandemic sits inside that window.

posts.title: Same app, different rules
posts.body:
A pupil can move from a school noticeboard into an algorithmic feed without anything telling them they have moved, and I do not know how you teach that.

It is the part of digital literacy I find hardest to put into a lesson, because the thing a child has to notice is the absence of a signal.

Meta says nearly 17,000 US schools are now in its School Partnership Program, and that it is expanding from a reporting route into school Channels, Stories, clubs, teams, directories and verified school communities.

The case for it is real and I am not going to skip past it. Schools already struggle to reach pupils across half a dozen systems nobody checks. If teenagers are in the app anyway, a verified school space beats another portal, and a direct line to the platform helps a school deal with things that cross the gate.

This is a company announcement about a US programme. It is not evidence that putting school communities inside a social app makes pupils safer, or less safe, and I would not use it as either.

But hold the phone the way a fifteen year old holds it.

The school Story sits in the same app as the group chat, the creator they follow, the recommendation feed, and whatever the algorithm decides comes next. Same device, same icon, four completely different sets of rules about who can see them and who decides what they see.

Our instinct has always been to teach children about apps. Instagram is risky. The school platform is fine. That holds up until the boundary runs through the middle of one app, and then it teaches a child nothing at all.

So the thing our lessons ask is not which app you are in. It is which kind of space. Who can see this. Who controls it. Why am I being shown this particular thing. What happens if I reply. When does this need an adult.

A phone free lesson is still a sensible boundary. It just cannot teach the decision at four fifteen, when the boundary has gone.

One swipe apart, two different places. Repost this if schools should be teaching that difference.

How does your school teach the difference between a school space and an open feed, when they are one swipe apart?
posts.comment: Meta's announcement was made on 29 September 2026 and the figure of nearly 17,000 schools is the company's own, in a US programme. Worth being clear what it is not: there is no independent evidence yet on whether school communities inside the app improve communication or safeguarding outcomes, and I am not claiming either direction. The reason I think it matters is narrower and it would matter without Meta: platform categories are collapsing, so "which app" is becoming a worse question than "which kind of space". Our schools scheme teaches that as context rather than as an approved app list, mapped to Education for a Connected World and the 2025 RSHE guidance, at guidedchildhood.com/schools.

posts.title: How would you test readiness
posts.body:
I have built a product around the word readiness and I still cannot tell you how to test it.

That is the uncomfortable centre of this, and picking a better age does not make it go away.

Everyone argues about the number. Thirteen for an account. Sixteen for social media. Eighteen for an AI companion. I understand why. An age is enforceable, auditable, the same for every child, and a regulator can write it down.

What an age cannot do is describe the child in front of you.

A child can turn thirteen without knowing that an AI which sounds caring does not care. Without understanding that a chatbot can be confidently wrong about something it has no business being confident about. Without noticing when a conversation is being kept going rather than finished. With no idea when to stop talking to a machine and go and find a person.

So what would a readiness test actually look like.

Not a quiz. A child can pass a quiz on Monday and hand over their address on Friday. Not a certificate either, because the whole point is that it moves as they grow and as the technology does.

The closest I have got is three things a parent can see for themselves. Can the child explain, in their own words, why this thing is showing them this. Can they tell you about a time they stopped. And do they come to you when something turns, which depends entirely on whether coming to you went well enough last time that they would do it again.

That last one is the real test, and it is not about the child at all.

Our stage check is an attempt at this and I will not dress it up as more. Three questions about your own child, and a stage with the things worth practising next. A starting point rather than a measurement. We have no outcome evidence that a child who finishes a stage behaves differently afterwards, and almost nobody in this field does.

An age tells you when the door opens. It tells you nothing about who walks through it.

If you had to judge whether a child was ready for something online, what would you actually look at?
posts.comment: Nothing in this one is a research finding and I want to be straight about that. There is no validated readiness instrument for children and digital environments that I am aware of, which is the problem rather than an oversight on my part. The three signals above are my own working answer from building this, not a measure anybody has tested. If you know of serious work on assessing digital readiness rather than digital knowledge, I would genuinely like to read it, because I have looked and come up fairly empty. The stage check is at guidedchildhood.com/starter-pack if you want to see what our attempt looks like.

posts.title: Two children, same game
posts.body:
Two children can both say "I'm playing Minecraft" and have almost nothing in common.

I cannot tell you which one is fine. That is the hardest thing to answer for a parent, and the age rating on the box does not answer it either.

Australia's eSafety Commissioner used legally enforceable notices to ask Roblox, Minecraft, Fortnite and Steam what they actually do to protect children. The answers describe four quite different safety systems sitting behind four things that all look, from a kitchen table, like "they're on a game".

During the period covered, Epic and Mojang still relied on a user declaring their own age at sign up. Somebody declaring 18 could reach higher risk communication features without a further check, which in Minecraft could include third party unmoderated servers. Valve relied on self declared age for Steam and did not collect age information at all. Roblox had gone further, bringing in stronger age assurance for some higher risk features in Australia from December 2025.

This is a transparency report, not an outcomes study. It does not show that one platform causes more harm than another and I will not use it that way. It is also Australian, and UK configurations and duties differ.

But it does retire the question parents keep being asked to answer. Not "is this game safe", which nobody can tell you, but what can my child actually do in here.

Who can contact them. Whether a conversation can move somewhere private. Whether the space is moderated. Whether the service has any idea how old they are. Whether they know how to block, report and tell someone.

Which is why our schools scheme is built on capability rather than an approved app list, and why DiGi will not answer "is X safe for my child" with a yes or a no. It asks the mode, the chat settings, who can make contact and what the child can already handle, then gives you a pathway rather than a verdict.

The platform carries the first responsibility here. An age rating still cannot teach a child what to do when the room changes around them.

Same game, nothing else the same. Worth a repost if that is useful to a parent.

What do you ask before you say yes to a game?

It is a compliance and transparency comparison built from what the providers told the regulator, not a measurement of harm, and I am not ranking the four. eSafety's earlier work found 40 percent of Australian children aged 8 to 17 played online with people they did not know offline, and that is Australian, so do not transpose it to the UK. The capability version for parents is at guidedchildhood.com/starter-pack.

posts.title: The rule I could actually enforce
posts.body:
I set a timer because it was the rule I could actually enforce.

That is the honest reason, and it took me a while to admit it. A time limit is checkable. I could look at a clock and know whether I had done my job. Who my child was talking to was a much harder question, so I asked it less often.

Ofcom published Growing Up Gaming yesterday, and the numbers have a version of that in them.

Among parents whose children play games, 64% said talking to strangers worried them. Among children who game online, 55% said they at least sometimes play with people they have never met offline.

Only 43% set any rule about who their child can play with. Time limits ran at 56%.

I am not going to turn that into a neat twelve point gap, because those figures come from different questions and different groups and the arithmetic would be dishonest. What it does show is which rule an adult reaches for first.

Two children, both an hour.

One is building something with a school friend whose mum you have met at the gate.

The other is talking to someone they met inside the game, who has started asking them to carry it on somewhere private.

Same hour. Nothing else the same.

The part that costs me goes here. Someone your child met online is not automatically a threat. Ofcom's own figures say 96% of children who game online play with friends or family at least sometimes, and the report describes gaming as a real way to socialise and make things. I am not arguing against online friends.

I am arguing that a timer cannot tell a child who is trustworthy, why somebody wants secrecy, or that a conversation has quietly changed under them.

And none of it is a parent's job alone. The platforms carry a legal duty here that no amount of good parenting replaces.

But tonight, four questions beat the clock.

Who are you playing with. How do you know them. Can they reach you outside the game. What would make you leave and come and tell me.

Repost this if the rule you enforce is not the one that worries you most.

Which of those four has your family actually had?

All self reported, none of it causal. The counterweight is in the same report: 96% of children who game online play with friends or family at least sometimes, and Ofcom describes gaming as a genuine way to socialise, learn and create. Parent rules do not replace what the Online Safety Act requires of the platforms.

posts.title: Four thousand teenagers are about to test what argument cannot
posts.body:
I have been arguing about this for years on evidence that cannot settle it, and so has almost everybody else.

Which is why Bradford matters if you have a child between twelve and fifteen.

The IRL Trial has moved into schools. Year groups are being assigned either a daily social media limit with an overnight curfew, or their usual use, for six weeks, and researchers will compare anxiety, sleep, bullying, and time spent with friends and family. It is led from Bradford with Amy Orben at Cambridge, funded by Wellcome.

Nearly everything the rest of us quote, me included, shows an association. This is built to show what changes when use actually goes down.

That is a different thing, and I have quietly wanted somebody to do it for a long time.

The fair objection is that families and regulators cannot sit still waiting for perfect evidence about risks we already know are there, and that six weeks will not answer every question about every child. Both true. It can still trade some of our confidence for a measurement, which I will take.

The result worth reading will not be the headline either. It will be underneath it. Did they sleep more. Did anxiety move. Did they spend the time with people, or move to a different screen.

There are no results yet. Anyone telling you this proves limits work, or proves they do not, has not read it.

And here is the part nobody can hand to the researchers. A limit changes access. It does not teach judgement. If a child gets six quieter weeks, something has to happen in the quiet, or they come out of it with the same instincts and a worse temper.

That is the argument I would rather we were having.

Better a trial than another round of the same argument. Repost it.

What would you want them to measure before anybody calls it a success?

Wellcome funded at £1.2 million from April 2026, with support from the NIHR Yorkshire and Humber ARC. The primary outcome is self reported anxiety, with sleep, bullying, body image, school life and time with friends and family alongside it. Two things I am not stating, because I could not find either: an end date, and when it reports. I looked twice. It is a cap and a curfew rather than a full ban, so it is not a referendum on the Government's policy. When results do come, adherence, other devices in the house, and what the time got spent on instead will all matter more than the top line.

posts.title: The film is dramatic. The design problem is real.
posts.body:
I have watched a feed narrow in my own house and I still could not tell you the moment it turned.

That is the honest problem with this, and it is why a film about it is so tempting. A film gives you the moment. A villain, a decision, a turn.

The Social Reckoning is in UK cinemas now, built on Frances Haugen's disclosures and the Facebook Files reporting. That spine is real. The dialogue is not. Timelines compressed, characters composited, an institutional failure given a cast you can look at.

None of which makes the problem underneath it fictional.

Ofcom says personalised recommendations are a main route by which children meet harmful content. Its own evidence also refuses to let me round that up: recommender systems are not inherently harmful, they help people find useful things, and the risk comes from repetition, combination and intensity rather than from the existence of a feed.

The same care belongs with Molly Russell. The coroner did not find that one app or one algorithm killed her. The conclusion was that she died from an act of self harm while suffering from depression and the negative effects of online content.

Accuracy is not softness here. It is the only thing that puts the responsibility where it belongs, with the people who choose the design and the people who regulate it, rather than with a tired parent at nine at night.

Which still leaves the child who is in the feed today.

I keep coming back to the fact that I could not name the turn in my own house. So the thing worth teaching is not what an algorithm is. It is the noticing. This is getting narrower. This is getting darker. I did not choose this and it seems to know what is coming next.

Then pause, stop feeding it, reset the recommendations, leave rather than try to outscroll it, and tell somebody.

A situation a child can learn to interrupt is worth more than a diagram of how it works.

Repost this if you have watched a feed narrow and could not name the moment either.

What would tell you that a feed had started choosing for you?

Molly Russell's inquest conclusion is the Chief Coroner's own wording and I have not shortened it. Ofcom's Children's Register of Risks is where the recommender finding comes from, and the same document is clear that these systems are not inherently harmful, which is a qualification I would rather state than have pointed out to me. The five steps are a rehearsal, not proven protection, and nothing a child does replaces a platform's duty to make the design safer. Our schools pilot is at schools.guidedchildhood.com/pilot.

posts.title: Fifteen minutes is not a safety test
posts.body:
Teenagers using ChatGPT's teen mode spend under fifteen minutes a day, OpenAI says. I honestly do not know whether that should reassure me.

That is OpenAI's own figure, published on 7 October, alongside another: less than 2 per cent interact for over three straight hours. I could not find how many teens it covers or over what period. I have no reason to doubt either number. They answer a question about time.

I use AI most days now. On morning walks I used to listen to podcasts and watch AI built software get better, and then I found I could turn the system in my head into something real without a team. How long I spend with it tells you almost nothing. What I ask it to do tells you nearly everything.

Common Sense Media published its own assessment of ChatGPT for Teens the same week, built on more than 4,000 test prompts. Its testers found that refusals of explicit sexual role play held. They also reported that no parental alert fired in their dedicated test, that adult registered accounts never moved into the teen experience even when the tester said they were 13, and that study controls could be bypassed.

OpenAI disputes some of it. It told Common Sense that parent and teen accounts must be linked for about three hours before alerts can be sent. Common Sense says it stands by its reading.

Common Sense is funded in part by tech companies including OpenAI, which is worth saying out loud.

Adversarial testing hunts for failure. It cannot tell you how often an ordinary teenager meets one, and none of this shows that typical AI use harms young people.

But picture two teenagers, fifteen minutes each. One gets feedback on a science draft. The other is telling it something they have not told anyone.

The clock reads the same.

I am drafting a short set of questions about purpose, privacy, proof and the way back to a trusted adult. It is not built yet. Sources are in the first comment.

What a child asks an AI tells you more than how long they spend. Repost it.

If you asked your teenager what job they gave AI this week, what do you think they would say?

posts.title: The risk assessment belongs before the feature
posts.body:
I cannot tell you whether Instagram's disappearing photos are a risk to children. Ofcom cannot tell you yet either, and I think that is the interesting part.

Ofcom has opened a formal investigation into Meta. It asks whether the risks to children were properly assessed before the feature, called Instants, went live in May. It does not say the feature has harmed anyone.

Meta says the risks were assessed. It told Reuters it briefed Ofcom several times before launch, and its account of Instants is that screenshots, reshares and forwarding are blocked, there is no public feed and Teen Account protections apply. That is a real answer, and Ofcom has not ruled on it either way.

What I keep turning over is the order.

Most child safety I have watched arrives second. A feature ships, a problem appears, and then adults add a warning, a setting or a lesson. The Online Safety Act asks for the reverse. Assess the risk first, and update the assessment before a significant change.

Schools live the small version of this. An app is approved in September. In March it adds something new, and the September approval is still in a drawer, answering a question nobody is asking any more.

So these are the four questions I would put to any new feature before a child meets it.

What behaviour could this encourage?

What might disappear from an adult's view?

Could a child mistake privacy for safety?

What happens when it goes wrong, and who do they tell?

I want Guided Childhood to put the same four to anything we add.

Nothing here says Instagram is unsafe or that its safeguards fail. Nobody has shown that yet.

The Ofcom announcement and the Reuters report are in the first comment.

Repost this if the assessment belongs before the feature rather than after the problem.

When an app your school already approved changes what it does, who decides whether to look again?

posts.title: Europe drew a staircase
posts.body:
Nobody has told me what a twelve year old should be able to do by the time they turn thirteen.

That is the gap I keep falling into, and Europe has just made it a much more concrete question.

The proposed EU KIDS Act would build a staircase rather than a wall. No social media account under 13. At 13 and 14, a parent sets up a limited account with parental tools always on, approved contacts, and no more than an hour a day. From 15, an independent account, with the service still carrying its safety by design duties.

It also goes after the mechanics rather than just the age. For minors it would restrict infinite scroll, autoplay, streaks and attention pulling notifications, require recommenders to prioritise safety and quality over engagement, and prohibit AI systems from using designs that simulate a human relationship in ways likely to create emotional dependency.

The objection goes first, because it is a fair one. Thirteen, fifteen and one hour are blunt numbers. Children develop differently. A law like this can leave everyone feeling that an age has settled a readiness question it has not touched. The Commission does not claim otherwise, and I am not going to pretend Europe has proved our approach right.

But the shape matters, and it is the shape we are heading for too. The UK confirmed its own under 16 restrictions in June, expected in spring 2027.

So here is the question a staircase creates, and I have not seen anybody answer it.

A protected twelve year old does not become a prepared fifteen year old. The protection buys you years. It does not fill them.

What should a child be able to do before the next step? Recognise persuasive design. Explain why a feed chose that particular thing. Hold a group conversation when it turns. Protect their own information. Notice an AI starting to behave like a relationship. Know when something has to come back to an adult.

That is what our pathway is built to stage, which is why it is organised around what a child can do rather than the birthday that unlocks an app.

The Commission is taking feedback from children, parents, teachers and schools until 26 November. Six weeks. School leaders are exactly who it needs to hear from and exactly who tends not to reply to these.

The window shuts on 26 November, so repost this while a reply still counts.

If access becomes staged, what should children be taught at each stage?

The specifics above on parental tools always on, the daily limit and parental approval of contacts come from the Commission's own FAQ. On the UK side, the under 16 restrictions were confirmed on 15 June 2026 and are expected in spring 2027, with default protections for 16 and 17 year olds alongside. The staircase framing, and the argument that the teaching should mirror the access, are mine rather than the Commission's.

posts.title: The safety feature is not the outcome
posts.body:
Here is something I cannot prove about my own product, and I would rather say it than have somebody find it.

I do not yet know whether a child who finishes one of our stages behaves differently afterwards. We measure what a parent reports, and whether a lesson was genuinely passed rather than tapped through. We do not have outcome evidence. Almost nobody in this field does, and that is the whole problem.

Meta, TikTok and X have been in the Administrative Court in London challenging how much information Ofcom can demand under the Online Safety Act. The requests reportedly include how much content was removed or restricted and, the part I care about, how many users were actually exposed to harmful material. The companies argue the requests are too broad and too burdensome. Ofcom says it needs the data to judge whether the regime works, and says it narrowed the scope.

Their argument is not frivolous. A regulator should have to say why it needs data, requests should be proportionate, and producing granular numbers across enormous services is genuinely hard. This was a dispute about the reach of an information power, not a finding that anybody breached a child safety duty.

Underneath it is the question that catches everyone, us included.

An age check can exist. A parental control can exist. A reporting button can exist. A rule can exist.

Did fewer children encounter the thing. Did reporting get easier. How fast was it dealt with. Did it work the same way for a nine year old as for a fifteen year old.

"Safety feature introduced" can hide whether the feature changed anything, the same way "screen time" hides what a child was doing and "social media" hides four different products with four different designs.

So every stage we write has to finish a sentence: after this, the child should be able to recognise, explain or do what. Not "we covered privacy". We judge our own films on how many people started a stage check, never on views, for exactly the same reason.

Repost it if a safety measure should have to say what a child can do afterwards.

If you work in a school or in safeguarding: when you bring in a digital safety measure, what do you measure afterwards to know whether it helped?

To be clear about what it was and was not: a challenge to the scope and proportionality of an information gathering power, not a ruling that any of the three has breached a child safety duty, and not evidence that the Act has improved or worsened anything for children. Ofcom's own May 2026 agreement with X, which set review time targets and quarterly reporting, is the nearest thing to what defined performance measurement looks like in practice.

posts.title: The child who never put them on
posts.body:
The most interesting child in the smart glasses argument is the one who never put them on.

I do not have a good answer for that child yet, and almost everything we teach is written for the other one. Do not share this. Do not film that. Check your settings. Ask first. All of it addressed to the child holding the device.

Norway has said it intends to propose temporary restrictions on AI glasses in privacy sensitive public places, with schools, nurseries, playgrounds and youth clubs among those being considered. A proposal, not a ban, and not here.

The other side deserves its due, because it is real. Meta has not ignored this. The glasses carry a recording light, and over the summer the system was strengthened so the camera is disabled if that light is covered or tampered with. There are genuine accessibility uses for wearable cameras, particularly for people who are blind or have low vision. A phone can record without consent too. None of this is new in kind.

What is different is who has to notice.

A phone camera changes the behaviour of the person holding it. They take it out and point it, and the act of recording is usually obvious. A camera built into something worn on a face changes the problem for everyone else in the room.

So the lesson has to run both ways. Does a child know what a light on a pair of glasses means. Would they feel able to say they do not want to be recorded. What happens in a changing room, a playground, a corridor. Who do they tell when a recording gets shared.

That is a privacy and consent capability, and in our scheme privacy and consent are taught years before independent access, because the bystander version of this does not wait for a child to own the device.

Our lessons currently teach a child to use a camera well. They do not yet teach a child how to stand in front of one. That is the gap I am working on this term.

How are schools handling the child who is not wearing them?

posts.title: The relationship with no friction
posts.body:
I do not know what a child learns from a relationship where the other side never gets tired of them.

That is the question I cannot answer, and I have stopped treating it as the same question as whether a child might mistake an AI for a friend. It runs the other way. Not what the machine says to the child. What the child practises when they talk back to it.

Researchers at the University of Washington and Rutgers watched eight children aged 6 to 11 play with generative AI toys. The children started socially, asking names and birthdays. When the toys kept failing to understand them, some began testing them, provoking them, speaking to them in ways they probably would not use on another child in the room.

Eight children, two sessions. That tells us nothing about whether AI toys make children aggressive or wear down empathy, and I would not use it that way.

It did change what I think AI literacy has to cover.

A human relationship has friction in it. Someone gets bored. Someone disagrees. Someone says that is enough. Someone can be hurt. A child learns slowly and badly that another person has needs that exist whether or not they are convenient.

An AI has no feelings to hurt. It can now perform the entire language of a relationship with none of the stakes underneath it.

So our AI module does not only ask whether the answer is true. It asks why the machine is answering like a person, what it remembers, whether you would speak to a person this way, and when a conversation should stop being with a machine and start being with a human. DiGi runs to the same rule: it never claims to need the child, and never sets itself up as the relationship that understands them best.

I would rather teach the friction than assume children will not go looking for the thing that has none.

Teach the friction, rather than assume they will not go looking. Repost this if that lands.

It cannot estimate how common any of it is and it does not establish developmental harm. posts.title: A photograph is information
posts.body:
I cannot tell a parent the chance that a photograph of their child will be misused. Nobody can, and the number I am about to give you does not answer it either.

The Internet Watch Foundation assessed 6,310 AI generated images in the first six months of this year that met the legal definition of child sexual abuse. Across the whole of 2025 the figure was 4,512. Where age and gender were recorded, 98 percent showed girls, and nearly four in five showed children aged 7 to 13.

Before anything else: that is a count of images, not a count of children, and it is not a risk estimate for a family photo. It does not show that posting a picture of your child causes this material to be made. I will not use it to frighten parents into deleting their albums, and the IWF does not use it that way either.

What it does show is that the environment around a child's image has changed. Some of this material is wholly synthetic. Some is made by altering real pictures of real children. Once an image exists, what can be done to it is not what it was five years ago.

The responsibility here sits overwhelmingly with platforms, model developers, regulators and adults. The IWF is arguing for the ability to detect material nobody has seen before, because a newly made image has no fingerprint until somebody finds and assesses it. That is the right fight and it is not a child's to win.

What a child can have is language for their own image. A nine year old does not need a lecture on generative models. They can understand that a photograph is information about them. That sharing it creates an audience. That people should ask first. That they are allowed to say no. And that if an image is altered or used to humiliate them, the first job is to tell an adult rather than carry it alone.

Which is why personal information and privacy sit in the early stages of the passport, years before social media independence. Image consent belongs in exactly the same place.

Repost it if more parents should hear that a photograph is information.

When did your school, or your family, first teach a child that their picture is part of their digital life?

It counts images assessed, not unique children, and detection practice affects the count, so the rise is not a clean incidence measure. This material is already criminal in the UK. posts.title: AI literacy needs somebody to own it
posts.body:
A child cannot spot a confident wrong answer in a subject they know nothing about. That is the part of AI literacy I have no neat solution for, and it is why the phrase makes me uneasy.

Mearns Castle High School in East Renfrewshire has appointed Jamie Laycock as Principal Teacher of AI Literacy, believed to be the first dedicated post of its kind in the UK. S1 and S2 get dedicated lessons. Older pupils meet it through citizenship and personal education, with an elective for seniors. The teaching reported so far covers synthetic images, fabricated answers, bias, anthropomorphism, and the habit chatbots have of agreeing with you.

The cautious case goes first. One appointment proves nothing about outcomes. Another specialist post is not affordable in most schools. And AI should not become the fashionable subject that crowds out reading and subject knowledge, because critical thinking does not float free of knowing things. A pupil checking an AI claim needs something to check it against.

Which is the argument for progression rather than an assembly.

At one stage the question is whether you can tell this image might not be real. Later, whether you can check a claim against another source. Later again, whether you notice when a chatbot is flattering you, agreeing too readily, or starting to feel more like a person than it is.

Those capabilities travel. The tools will not stop changing.

Our schools scheme is built that way, 29 modules mapped to Education for a Connected World and the 2025 RSHE guidance, with the AI work staged across them rather than delivered in one talk, and a real pass rather than a tap through. I am not claiming it improves outcomes, because the pilot has not measured capability change yet. That is the honest position, and it is the same standard I would hold a school to.

I do not think every school now needs a Principal Teacher of AI Literacy. Mearns Castle has made the harder point: this needs curriculum time, progression, and somebody whose job it actually is.

Somebody should own AI literacy. Repost this if nobody owns it in your school.

posts.title: Ready for what
posts.body:
When my eldest started asking for a phone, I wanted an age. I assumed somebody had worked out the safe one.

Five years of reading this research later, I am fairly sure nobody has, and I am no longer sure the age is the useful question.

A study in JAMA Network Open followed 8,957 US adolescents. Owning a smartphone at 12 was associated with a 49 percent higher chance of reporting at least one eating disorder symptom two years later, after adjusting for symptoms already present at 12.

That deserves taking seriously, and the inconvenient part goes first. It does not show the phone caused anything. Ownership was not random. The researchers could not see what those children were actually doing on the phone. A symptom is not a diagnosis. And it is US data.

What it does expose is how much we compress into one word.

Getting a smartphone is not one change. It is private messaging. A camera in a bedroom. An algorithmic feed. Notifications after lights out. Appearance content. Friends. Homework. Independence. All of it arriving on the same afternoon under a single question: what age.

The question I find more useful is, ready for what.

So the stage check asks three things about your actual child instead of handing you a number. Their age, what you are dealing with right now, and how much time you can give it. Three questions, no sign up, and you get the stage with the things worth practising before independent access. Whether they can notice appearance pressure. Whether they understand why a feed keeps showing them more of something. Whether they know when to bring an adult in.

Delay buys you the space. It does not fill it.

Repost it if you wanted an age too, and found that nobody had worked one out.

What did you decide in the end, and would you decide it the same way again?
